title: Sand Cartels: Illegal Dredging in Southeast Asia and Coastal Displacement
subtitle: How Singapore's land reclamation ambitions are displacing coastal communities across the Mekong Delta — and why current solutions are failing.
excerpt: An estimated 20 to 50 million Bangladeshis are projected to be displaced from coastal areas due to river erosion by 2050. The relentless extraction of sand in Southeast Asia is leaving communities facing an uncertain future.

content.text: In my house, the walls were filled with sand for more than half the height. One night, I lost everything. Now I have no place to stay.
content.attribution: Local housewife, Rojoniline village, northern Bangladesh

content.text: Her family was forced to leave their home after sediment-heavy flash floods — driven by unchecked sand mining in the area — overwhelmed their village. This is just one example among countless cases of displacement caused by sand mining worldwide.

content.label: Bangladeshis projected to be displaced from coastal areas due to river erosion by 2050

content.text: The relentless extraction of sand in Southeast Asia is leaving communities like Rojoniline facing an uncertain future, only to fulfill Singapore's land reclamation ambitions. As a key source for its artificial land expansion, Singapore's high demand for imported sand from countries like Cambodia and Indonesia has led to excessive sand mining, causing land loss and forced displacement.
The Expense Beneath a Growing Nation

Between 1997 and 2017, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, and Vietnam — historically Singapore's largest sand exporters — banned sand exports due to environmental concerns. However, Singapore, having spent another $57.5 million on sand imports in 2023, has continued prioritizing land reclamation as a driver of economic and infrastructural development since independence.

To achieve its goal of expanding to 766 square kilometers by 2030, the country has increasingly relied on illegal channels to meet its growing sand demand. In Vietnam, investigative journalist Le Dinh Tuyen uncovered that licensed mining operations in the Mekong Delta met only 10–20% of actual market demand, suggesting that most sand extraction occurs illegally through unregulated dredging.

content.caption: A hopper dredger 'rainbows' dredged sand onto a forming coastline.

content.label: Major erosion hotspots recorded in Vietnam in 2023, spanning 741 kilometers

content.text: Between 2018 and 2022, 2,500 houses were swept away across An Giang, Dong Thap, Can Tho, Vinh Long, and Ca Mau provinces. These losses disrupted rural livelihoods, damaged infrastructure, and forced families into precarious relocation.

The illicit sand trade thrives on economic incentives, technical loopholes, and institutional gaps. The primary driver is soaring demand for Singapore's land reclamation, propelling sand consumption and market value to an expected 955 million tons and $28.6 billion by 2035.

Institutional weaknesses, including fragmented jurisdiction and corruption, reinforce these illegal activities. Provincial governments often act in isolation with minimal coordination, and in some cases, local officials have colluded with smugglers, issuing unauthorized permits or ignoring violations altogether.

content.alt: Aerial view of a dredging vessel dispersing sediment into turquoise coastal waters
content.caption: A dredging vessel disperses sediment plumes into coastal waters off the UAE.

content.text: In 2023, the UN Environment Programme launched Marine Sand Watch that uses satellite data to track dredging vessels and detect sand extraction within marine protected areas. However, Marine Sand Watch covers only about 60% of the global dredging fleet and lacks enforcement power, reducing its role to monitoring rather than prevention.
AIS vessel tracking can similarly be manipulated — vessels may disable transponders, falsify GPS data, or bypass detection entirely. Many local authorities also lack the resources to respond swiftly.
Beyond Surveillance: Structural and Systemic Strategies

A decentralized blockchain-based permit and tracking system can improve monitoring of illicit sand mining. Each shipment would be attached to a unique, immutable digital permit containing verifiable data such as extraction volume, coordinates, and time. Drones equipped with LiDAR and AI mapping can cross-check these parameters on-site, closing loopholes like forged invoices or disabled transponders.

Policymakers, especially in import-reliant nations like Singapore, must take responsibility not just for their supply chains but for the lives displaced in the process. Global stewardship of sand as a shared resource is no longer optional — it is urgent.
